name: Greyhairmaxxing

lead: Greyhairmaxxing is the practice of treating grey hair as an asset: leaving it undyed, or styling and toning it so it reads as a deliberate silver look rather than something hidden. The appeal, as proponents describe it, is a distinguished, high-status appearance often summed up by the phrase "silver fox".

Grey hair comes from the loss of pigment-producing cells at the hair follicle and its timing is largely genetic. Discussion on looksmax.org centres on whether a man should dye or keep his grey in middle age, and on how age, hair density and the rest of the face affect how grey hair reads.

paras: In practice it means not colouring the hair, keeping the cut and grooming sharp so the grey looks intentional, and in some cases using toners or shampoos made to keep grey tones bright. Some people also use bleach and toner to create a silver shade on hair that is not yet grey.

Plain greying carries no health risk. Premature greying can be a family trait and is occasionally associated with medical conditions, in which case clinicians assess it. Bleaching hair to imitate silver can damage the hair and irritate the scalp.

angle.text: Proponents use grey hair as a style asset, pairing it with good grooming and a fitting cut so it reads as intentional. The look is usually discussed for men in their 30s and older.

lead: Greyhairmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for embracing grey or silver hair as a deliberate part of one's appearance instead of covering it. It is often framed through the "silver fox" ideal of an older man whose grey hair signals maturity and status.[1]

Grey hair results from a lack of pigment in the hair shaft, as melanocyte stem cells at the follicle die or stop producing new pigment cells; the age of onset appears to be largely genetic.[2] In looksmax.org discussion, members debate whether men should dye grey hair or keep it, with some arguing grey looks strong from roughly the 30s or 40s and others noting that dyed hair works best on someone who still looks young.[1]
infobox: Early to mid 20s in men, widely variable [2]

paras: The practice covers several behaviours: not dyeing naturally grey hair, adopting a short or neat cut meant to flatter grey, and, for those not yet grey, bleaching and toning to a silver shade. The common thread is presenting grey as a chosen look.
Related terms include "silver fox", used in popular slang for an attractive older man with grey hair.

Grey or white hair is hair that lacks melanin; it appears pale because of how light reflects from unpigmented keratin rather than because of a grey pigment.[2][3] Greying begins at the root, and new hair can emerge grey while neighbouring follicles still produce pigmented hair.[3]

Wikipedia reports that greying typically begins in the early to mid twenties for men, that over 60% of Americans have some grey hair by 40, and that onset age is almost entirely genetic.[2] A 2016 study of about 6,000 people in Latin America identified the IRF4 gene as associated with greying, and a 1996 BMJ study linked smoking with earlier greying.[3] Stress is popularly blamed; the evidence is described as limited, although a 2020 Nature study in rats found an immune-driven loss of melanocyte stem cells.[3]

A looksmax.org thread titled "Greyhairmaxxing or not?" has the original poster asking whether a man should dye or keep grey hair in middle age, reasoning that darker hair makes a person look more "haloed" and wanting a plan in advance.[1] Replies advise focusing on one's 20s and 30s, say that dyed hair needs a youthful face to work, and suggest "greymaxx, moneymaxx" and status-building instead; another reply says grey can look very good from around 30-40 onward, while a poster with a family history of premature greying on the maternal side asks what happens if it comes early.[1]

No studies found. Research on the biology of greying exists (see Biology of grey hair) but no trial has examined grey hair as a styling choice or its effect on perceived attractiveness in this context.[3]

lore.intro: The topic appears as a planning question on looksmax.org about how men should handle hair colour with age.[1]
